question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother with a history of multiple falls for the last 8 months. He was born at term without any perinatal complications. At birth, his weight and height were 57th and 62nd percentile for his age, respectively. For the first year, he had normal developmental milestones. He started walking at the age of 17 months and started climbing stairs at 2 years of age. For the last 8–10 months, he has been walking clumsily, has fallen multiple times, and is having difficulty standing from the sitting position. He is not able to climb the stairs now. Past medical history is unremarkable. His vaccinations are up-to-date. His maternal uncle had a similar history, and he became bed-bound at 12 years of age. During the physical examination, the patient stood up from sitting position slowly by placing hands on his knees. What additional findings will be present in this patient?

options.opb: Inability to release grasp after handshake
options.ope: Rash over shoulders and anterior chest

enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of the 4-year-old boy, including a history of multiple falls, clumsiness, difficulty standing from a sitting position, and a family history of similar symptoms, strongly suggests a neuromuscular disorder, likely muscular dystrophy. This condition is characterized by proximal muscle weakness, which aligns with the observed difficulty in climbing stairs and the slow rise from a sitting position. Pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles is a classic finding in muscular dystrophy due to the replacement of muscle tissue with fat and connective tissue. Therefore, the most relevant and consensus-supported additional finding in this patient would be pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles. Other options, such as early contractures or rash, do not align with the typical presentation of muscular dystrophy in this context.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 4-year-old boy, including a history of multiple falls, clumsiness, difficulty standing from a sitting position, and a family history of similar symptoms, strongly suggests a neuromuscular disorder, likely muscular dystrophy. In particular, the symptoms align with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), which is characterized by proximal muscle weakness and is often associated with pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles due to the replacement of muscle tissue with fat and connective tissue. This finding is a classic manifestation of DMD and is consistent with the boy's symptoms and family history. Other options, such as early contractures or rash, do not align with the typical presentation of muscular dystrophy in this context. Therefore, the most relevant and consensus-supported additional finding in this patient would be pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles.
